sweep_summary: Kera (kera1255) is in the catalog as no-word-stress on Pearce 2006 (Phonology). this search of works with stress in the title's four title hits are three Pearce works and one misassigned JASA paper. The 2007 UCL thesis (already held by the project, read: pp.27, 60, 92, 191, 333) states first-hand that overt stress plays no role and no syllable is more intense than the others, with prominence only at the head of iambic feet: confirms the catalog. The 2006 article's Crossref abstract ('Kera has no word-level stress') matches the catalog quote verbatim; its full text is paywalled and the archived author copy could not be re-downloaded (Internet Archive offline during this search of works with stress in the title). The 2013 CSLI book is the print version of the thesis (Harvard offsite only). Newman 2003 (JASA) is an English VOT/fricative study attached to Kera by a Glottolog machine assignment from the word 'evaluate': irrelevant. Extra: the catalog's secondary source Pearce 2007 ACAL 37 'Iambicity in Kera' was downloaded open from Cascadilla and also confirms (p.66: no overt stress in pitch or intensity; iambic feet with heavy heads). Pearce 2005 CamLing 'Iambicity without stress in Kera' remains unlocated. No change to the catalog's classification is warranted; the thesis can be added as a co-equal primary corroborating source.

new_statements.quote: Traditionally, the cue which is used the most as evidence for foot structure is the stress placed on head vowels. In Kera, stress is not particularly noticeable, and there is no pattern where one syllable is more intense than all the others giving rise to a word accent. Nevertheless, intensity is used at the level of the foot and this can be measured. The intensity is greater for the head of the foot. There is a consistent difference between heads and non-heads.
new_statements.citation: Pearce, Mary Dorothy (2007). The interaction of tone with voicing and foot structure: evidence from Kera phonetics and phonology. PhD thesis, University College London.
new_statements.reading: Kera has no word-level stress or word accent; there is foot-level prominence only (the head of each quantity-sensitive iambic foot is longer, more intense and has distinct vowel allophones), which is exactly the catalog's 'no-word-stress' coding. This is the full-length first-hand treatment behind the catalog's deciding 2006 Phonology article, by the same author and with the same instrumental evidence.

tone_statements.citation: Pearce, Mary (2011). Kera. Journal of the International Phonetic Association 41(2): 249-258 (Illustrations of the IPA). Cambridge University Press. doi:10.1017/S0025100311000168
tone_statements.quote: Most of the tone is lexical, but there is also some grammatical tone, most notably to distinguish between perfective and imperfective, though there are also segmental changes between these two forms. Some pronouns are also distinguished by tone. [...] In the Kera spoken by village women (and village men who are less influenced by French), there are three contrastive tones and no voicing contrast. In the speech varieties where French contact appears to play a role (in urban settings and among young males in the village), a voicing contrast has been reintroduced and the two lowest tones are pronounced at a similar or identical pitch.
tone_statements.locator: section 'Tone' and the following tone-and-voicing discussion (pp. 249-258)
tone_statements.summary: 3 contrastive level tones (H, M, L) in conservative Kera with no voicing contrast; L/M merged and cued by VOT in French-influenced (urban/young male) varieties; lexical plus some grammatical tone (aspect, pronouns); TBU syllable, only heavy syllables tonal in long words; no word stress (iambic feet).

tone_statements.citation: Pearce, Mary D. (2006). Enhancement between voice onset time (VOT) and F0: Evidence from Kera voicing perception. Journal of the Acoustical Society of America 119(5): 3269 (abstract, 151st Meeting of the ASA, Providence RI, special session on Enhancement and Multiplicity of Cues in Speech). doi:10.1121/1.4786136
tone_statements.quote: Previous research on production data from Kera (a Chadic tone language) has shown that tone plays a major contrastive role, whereas VOT has a lesser role which could indicate an ‘‘enhancing’’ relationship. ... For Kera, F0 is of major importance, while the VOT plays a lesser role in the judgment. ... in Kera, the tone is the main contrastive cue to voicing perception while the VOT values enhance the tone cues.
tone_statements.summary: Tonal per source; inventory not given. A perception study (15 Kera listeners, 200 PRAAT-manipulated tokens): F0/tone is the main voicing cue, VOT enhances it. Meeting abstract only.

tone_statements.citation: Hansson, Gunnar Ólafur (2004). Long-Distance Voicing Agreement: An Evolutionary Perspective. Proceedings of the 30th Annual Meeting of the Berkeley Linguistics Society (BLS 30), 130-141. Berkeley: Berkeley Linguistics Society. doi:10.3765/bls.v30i1.946
tone_statements.quote: As it turns out, there is extensive interaction between tone and laryngeal features in Kera, as in many other languages of the Chadic family (Ebert 1979a, b; Pearce 1998/99). More specifically, [voice] in obstruents frequently conditions Low tone. For example, in verbs, a root-initial voiced obstruent forces the following vowel to be L (6a) rather than M or H (6b)
tone_statements.locator: sec. 1.1.1 'Voicing Agreement and Tone-Voicing Interaction in Kera', p. 133
tone_statements.summary: Three tone levels (L, M, H) referenced; obstruent voicing conditions L on the following vowel; L-spreading to affixes; H-blocking; implosives and voiceless onsets pattern with M/H.

tone_statements.citation: Pearce, Mary (1998/1999). Consonants and tone in Kera (Chadic). Journal of West African Languages 27. pp. 33-70.
tone_statements.quote: Tone and grouping of consonants. There are three phonetic pitches in Kera: high (Hi), mid (M), and low (Lo). The surface melody of a word is influenced in two ways: (1) by the word-initial consonants or (2) by grammatical morphemes such as noun and verb affixes which can carry tone. ... Nouns have four possible underlying melodies: l, l h, h l, and h which are not predictable from the form of the word. Verbs, however, are underlyingly toneless.
tone_statements.locator: p. 35, sec. 0 Introduction, paragraph 'Tone and grouping of consonants'
tone_statements.summary: Hi/M/Lo called 'phonetic pitches', derived in register tier theory from registers h/l plus tones H/L; no tone glides; floating L on 2s -m, tonal definite article; variable M2 (h+L); 300+ forms.

tone_statements.locator: p. 35, sec. 0 Introduction, 'Tone and grouping of consonants'

tone_statements.citation: Wolff, Ekkehard (1987). Consonant-tone interference in Chadic and its implications for a theory of tonogenesis in Afroasiatic. In Daniel Barreteau (ed.), Langues et cultures dans le bassin du lac Tchad: journées d'études les 4 et 5 septembre 1984, ORSTOM Paris (Colloques et Séminaires), 193-216. Paris: Éditions de l'ORSTOM.
tone_statements.quote: The only East Chadic language that I know of for which consonant-tone interference has been explicitly described is Kera (EBERT 1979). Voiced obstruents function as depressors, the only "neutral" consonant is /h/, all others function as non-depressors. Cf. the tones on the first syllables of the "base" forms of the following verbs : depressor L gùsí "buy" L bèlè "love" non-depressor H pété "pluck (feathers)" H mánté "call" neutral L hèɗé "cut" H háté "learn" Cf. also the voiced/voiceless distinction of the simple as opposed to the plural verb bases which is paralleled by a Low/High distinction
tone_statements.summary: Only Low and High tones are named for Kera (depressor consonants -> L, others -> H; sg L vs pl H-H verb bases); no closed inventory, TBU or downstep statement; data second-hand from Ebert 1979.

tone_statements.citation: Ebert, Karen H. (1977). Some aspects of the Kera verbal system. In Martin Mould & Thomas J. Hinnebusch (eds), Papers from the Eighth Conference on African Linguistics (Studies in African Linguistics, Supplement 7), 33-41. Los Angeles: Department of Linguistics, University of California, Los Angeles. [whole-issue PDF on the SAL site, doi:10.32473/sal.v8iSupp.107646, pp. 37-45]
tone_statements.quote: Kera verbs exhibit the following tone patterns (for examples, see (1)): 1 ... A MM B HH C HH; 2a ... A LL B LH C LH; 2b ... A LL B LL C LH ... The A-forms are basic; high tones in B and C-forms are due to suffixes. ... The tone pattern which a verb follows is to a large extent predictable from initial consonants ... Kera verbs can thus be described in a 2-tone system: /+H/ always realized high /-H/ realized low after initial voiced C, mid elsewhere ... Thus, there are no lexical tone classes of verbs in Kera.
tone_statements.check: quotation verified in source (minor differences in wording)
tone_statements.summary: Verb tone only: surface H/M/L, underlying /+H/ vs /-H/ set by the initial consonant; a non-segmental H marks verbal noun/progressive (p.39); no language-wide tone inventory given.

tone_statements.citation: Remijsen, Bert & van Heuven, Vincent J. 2006. Introduction: between stress and tone. Phonology 23: 121-123. doi:10.1017/S0952675706000856
tone_statements.quote: The paper by Mary Pearce on Kera is of particular interest in this context. Kera is a tone language which has no culminative metrical prominence at the word level. (2) The classification rests on a 2006 peer-reviewed phonology article with instrumental data by the language's main specialist, corroborated by her held 409-pp 2007 PhD, which repeats 'no overt stress at the word level' in at least five places; this is the best available description of Kera prosody per the Glottolog bibliography (the only higher-page-count item, Ebert 1979, is an older impressionistic grammar). sources.citation: Pearce, Mary Dorothy (2007). The interaction of tone with voicing and foot structure: evidence from Kera phonetics and phonology. PhD thesis, University College London, xiii+409 pp. [Glottolog 15175]
sources.quote: [p.27] In most languages, any discussion of the foot structure will focus on the positioning of stress in the language. However, I cannot use stress as an indicator of the structure, because overt stress does not play a major role in the Kera system. [p.60] Traditionally, the cue which is used the most as evidence for foot structure is the stress placed on head vowels. In Kera, stress is not particularly noticeable, and there is no pattern where one syllable is more intense than all the others giving rise to a word accent. Nevertheless, intensity is used at the level of the foot and this can be measured. The intensity is greater for the head of the foot.
sources.locator: ch. 2 'Foot structure', sec. 2.1 p.27; sec. 2.2.4 'Intensity' p.60; also p.92, p.191, p.333
sources.note: First-hand, instrumental: Kera has no word-level stress/word accent; no syllable is more intense than all others. What exists is quantity-sensitive iambic foot structure whose heads carry greater intensity, duration and [-ATR] vowel allophony; the foot is the domain of vowel harmony and tone spreading and, in 3+-syllable words, the tone-bearing unit. p.92: 'Kera is unusual in being an example of an iambic language where stress has no role to play in the parsing of feet'; p.191: 'even without overt stress at the word level'.

sources.citation: Pearce, Mary (2007). Iambicity in Kera. In D. L. Payne & J. Peña (eds), Selected Proceedings of the 37th Annual Conference on African Linguistics, 66-76. Somerville, MA: Cascadilla. [catalog secondary source, not in target list; downloaded]
sources.quote: Although Afro-asiatic tone languages typically do not exhibit overt stress in the form of higher pitch or greater intensity, this paper will consider the evidence for a metrical system in Kera (an Eastern Chadic tone language spoken in southern Chad and parts of Cameroon, with 50,000 speakers (Ebert 1979; Pearce 1998, 2003, 2005, 2006)). Iambic feet are constructed over a combination of light and heavy syllables with an obligatory heavy syllable for the head of the foot.
sources.note: No overt stress (pitch or intensity) at word level; iambic feet with obligatory heavy heads, evidenced by vowel deletion/lengthening, allophony, harmony and tone spreading.
sources.venue: Selected Proceedings of the 37th Annual Conference on African Linguistics

sources.access_detail: open copy posted by the author (located 2026-09-25); a digital copy (available on request)
sources.quote: Kera has three distinct surface tones, H, M, and L, which in general correspond to the three underlying tones /H/, /M/, and /L/. All three surface tones appear in the tone patterns of nouns. (p. 64) ... The correlation between voicing and tone applies equally to verbs, which have the surface melodies H, M, L, and LH. (p. 66) ... Tone does spread in certain cases, but it does not skip syllables. (p. 79)
sources.note: Confirms the catalog tone class lexical-tone: three-way underlying /H/ /M/ /L/ contrast, seven noun melodies (H, M, L, LH, HL, MH, HM) and four verb melodies (H, M, L, LH), tone phonemic while obstruent VOT is a gradient phonetic enhancement cue (not [voice]); L tone spreads left onto the k- plural prefix, no long-distance spreading. Silent on word stress, feet, metrical structure and syllable weight: the words stress/foot/iamb/metrical do not occur in the text (only in a cited poster title), so it neither confirms nor contradicts the no-word-stress entry or its weight statement. sources.note: Argues Kera long-distance voicing agreement is a by-product of tone-voicing interaction: root-initial voiced obstruents force a following L (vs M or H after voiceless/implosive onsets) in verbs (ex. 6, 17) and nouns (ex. 18, from Pearce 1998/99); the voicing-induced L spreads to toneless affix vowels and can delink a suffixal H; two agreeing voiced obstruents are always separated by a L-toned rhyme and an intervening H blocks agreement (ex. 7); implosives do not correlate with L tone and are inert.
sources.venue: Proceedings of the 30th Annual Meeting of the Berkeley Linguistics Society (BLS 30)

tone.says: Argues Kera long-distance voicing agreement is a by-product of tone-voicing interaction: root-initial voiced obstruents force a following L (vs M or H after voiceless/implosive onsets) in verbs (ex. 6, 17) and nouns (ex. 18, from Pearce 1998/99); the voicing-induced L spreads to toneless affix vowels and can delink a suffixal H; two agreeing voiced obstruents are always separated by a L-toned rhyme and an intervening H blocks agreement (ex. 7); implosives do not correlate with L tone and are in…

sources.citation: Wolff, Ekkehard (1987). Consonant-tone interference in Chadic and its implications for a theory of tonogenesis in Afroasiatic. In Daniel Barreteau (ed.), Langues et cultures dans le bassin du lac Tchad: journées d'études les 4 et 5 septembre 1984, ORSTOM Paris (Colloques et Séminaires), 193-216. Paris: Éditions de l'ORSTOM.
sources.quote: The only East Chadic language that I know of for which consonant-tone interference has been explicitly described is Kera (EBERT 1979). Voiced obstruents function as depressors, the only "neutral" consonant is /h/, all others function as non-depressors. Cf. the tones on the first syllables of the "base" forms of the following verbs : depressor L gùsí "buy" L bèlè "love" non-depressor H pété "pluck (feathers)" H mánté "call" neutral L hèɗé "cut" H háté "learn" Cf. also the voiced/voiceless distinction of the simple as opposed to the plural verb bases which is paralleled by a Low/High distinction
sources.note: Only Low and High tones are named for Kera (depressor consonants -> L, others -> H; sg L vs pl H-H verb bases); no closed inventory, TBU or downstep statement; data second-hand from Ebert 1979.

sources.citation: Ebert, Karen H. (1977). Some aspects of the Kera verbal system. In Martin Mould & Thomas J. Hinnebusch (eds), Papers from the Eighth Conference on African Linguistics (Studies in African Linguistics, Supplement 7), 33-41. Los Angeles: Department of Linguistics, University of California, Los Angeles. [whole-issue PDF on the SAL site, doi:10.32473/sal.v8iSupp.107646, pp. 37-45]
sources.quote: Kera verbs exhibit the following tone patterns (for examples, see (1)): 1 ... A MM B HH C HH; 2a ... A LL B LH C LH; 2b ... A LL B LL C LH ... The A-forms are basic; high tones in B and C-forms are due to suffixes. ... The tone pattern which a verb follows is to a large extent predictable from initial consonants ... Kera verbs can thus be described in a 2-tone system: /+H/ always realized high /-H/ realized low after initial voiced C, mid elsewhere ... Thus, there are no lexical tone classes of verbs in Kera.
sources.note: Verb tone only: surface H/M/L, underlying /+H/ vs /-H/ set by the initial consonant; a non-segmental H marks verbal noun/progressive (p.39); no language-wide tone inventory given.

sources.citation: Pearce, Mary (2006). Evidence against voicing spread in Kera. In Richard Breheny & Mary Pearce (eds), UCL Working Papers in Linguistics 18, 345-355. London: Department of Phonetics and Linguistics, University College London.
sources.note: States Kera 'has three tones: L, M, and H' and argues that the long-distance voicing assimilation claimed for Kera (Odden 1994, Rose & Walker 2004, Uffmann 2003, from Ebert's data) is L-tone spreading: Kera has no distinctive [voice], VOT co-varies with F0, obstruents in L-toned syllables get short VOT (0-20 ms) perceived as voicing; evidence from the K-, -Ki/Ka, -T affixes, French loans and a lexicon count (9% voicing mismatches). Quotable (p.345): 'In this paper, I give evidence that the Kera spreading is tonal, and that Kera does not provide a case of voice spreading.'.
sources.venue: UCL Working Papers in Linguistics 18

tone.quote: Tone and grouping of consonants. There are three phonetic pitches in Kera: high (Hi), mid (M), and low (Lo). The surface melody of a word is influenced in two ways: (1) by the word-initial consonants or (2) by grammatical morphemes such as noun and verb affixes which can carry tone. ... Nouns have four possible underlying melodies: l, l h, h l, and h which are not predictable from the form of the word. Verbs, however, are underlyingly toneless.
tone.locator: p. 35, sec. 0 Introduction, paragraph 'Tone and grouping of consonants'
tone.summary: Hi/M/Lo called 'phonetic pitches', derived in register tier theory from registers h/l plus tones H/L; no tone glides; floating L on 2s -m, tonal definite article; variable M2 (h+L); 300+ forms.
